aboutPage.seoDescription: Who we are, how we work, and why transparent pricing and named specialists matter. Medical-travel coordination across 9 destinations.
aboutPage.lede: We're a medical-travel coordinator — not a hospital, not an insurer, not an advertising network. Patients come to us when they need surgery or a second opinion abroad, and we sit between them and the hospitals so the paperwork, the pricing, and the logistics don't become someone's second full-time job.
aboutPage.pWhatWeDo: When a patient contacts us, we match them with 3-5 hospitals that fit their condition, budget, and visa situation. We request written quotes, present them side-by-side, and hand-hold visa paperwork, travel booking, and post-discharge follow-up. The hospital bills the patient directly; we take a coordination fee from the hospital, disclosed up front. No markups, no hidden commissions layered onto the treatment price.
aboutPage.pWhatWeDont: We don't practise medicine. We don't diagnose. We don't pick your surgery. When our medical panel writes a second opinion, it's written and signed by a named board-certified specialist at a partner hospital — not by us, and not by a language model. If a case is outside our panel's expertise, we say so and decline it the same day.
aboutPage.pVetting1: Every hospital on MedCasts is either JCI-accredited, NABH-accredited (for India), or holds the equivalent national certification. We cross-check against the accrediting body's live registry at listing time and re-check annually. Hospitals that lose accreditation are removed within 30 days of the status change.
aboutPage.pVetting2: Pricing is requested in writing per case; we don't publish numbers that haven't been confirmed by the hospital's own IPD (International Patient Department). The price bands you see on destination and cost pages are sampled from partner-hospital quote sheets across a rolling six-month window.
aboutPage.pRecords: Medical files you upload are encrypted in transit and at rest. Access is limited to the specific case manager and the reviewing physicians assigned to your case. Records are purged 30 days after we deliver an opinion or after your treatment is complete, whichever is later. We'll sign an NDA on request and support data-export requests within 7 working days. Regulatory posture: GDPR-aligned for EU patients, HIPAA-adjacent for US patients (we're not a Covered Entity, but our Business Associate agreements with US hospital partners cover the handover).
aboutPage.pContent1: Our pages fall into two buckets. First: structured directory data — hospitals, doctors, treatments, prices. This is sourced from hospital websites, public registries (Wikipedia, Wikidata, government portals), and hospital-supplied quote sheets, then templated into reading copy. Second: editorial content — blog posts, visa guides, destination overviews, second-opinion FAQs. Editorial content is drafted in-house and reviewed by a practising specialist before it ships. See our
aboutPage.pBase: Operations run out of offices in India and the UAE, with local contract coordinators in Turkey, Thailand, Germany, and Singapore. Most case managers are clustered in Bangalore and Dubai, so response times outside 08:00-22:00 IST are slower on non-emergency inquiries.
aboutPage.limitsBoxText: MedCasts is a coordinator, not a clinician. Information on these pages is general. Anything specific to your case — surgery risk, prognosis, medication interactions — comes from the treating physician, in writing, signed. We'll help you get that in front of you. We won't replace it.

termsPage.seoDescription: MedCasts terms: who we are, what we do and do not do, how we are paid, and the honest boundaries of a medical-travel coordinator.
termsPage.lede: The honest boundaries of what a medical-travel coordinator can and cannot do for you. Read before you engage our case managers.
termsPage.body1: MedCasts ("we", "us", "our") operates a medical-travel coordination platform connecting international patients with accredited hospitals. We are coordinators, not clinicians. We don't practice medicine, diagnose conditions, or prescribe treatment.
termsPage.bullets2Item1: Match you to 1–3 hospitals appropriate for your clinical situation and budget.
termsPage.bullets2Item2: Coordinate itemized quotes, treatment plans, and surgeon communications.
termsPage.bullets2Item3: Handle visa invitation letters, travel logistics, accommodation, and interpreter support.
termsPage.bullets2Item4: Provide a named case manager from first contact through 90-day post-op follow-up.
termsPage.bullets2Item5: Coordinate free second opinions from our medical panel of senior specialists.
termsPage.bullets3Item1: **We don't practice medicine.** Our case managers, researchers, and the information on this site are not a substitute for a doctor-patient relationship.
termsPage.bullets3Item2: **We don't prescribe.** No medication recommendations, dosages, or clinical judgments.
termsPage.bullets3Item3: **We don't guarantee outcomes.** Every surgery has risk. We surface hospitals with strong track records; we can't promise results.
termsPage.bullets3Item4: **We don't replace your local doctor.** You should keep your local physician informed throughout.
termsPage.body4Para1: Hospitals pay us a coordination fee after you choose to proceed — typically 5–15% of the hospital's gross invoice. This is disclosed on every quote we send. You don't pay us anything directly. Second opinions, quote preparation, and pre-travel coordination are free to you whether or not you book.
termsPage.body4Para2: This means: our incentive to send you to a hospital increases with the hospital's invoice. We counter this structurally by (a) running an independent medical panel whose second-opinion compensation is flat per case, and (b) publishing our editorial policy including the 28% of oncology cases where we recommend against surgery.
termsPage.bullets5Item1: Give us accurate clinical information. Omissions (prior surgery, current medications, allergies) can directly affect your safety.
termsPage.bullets5Item2: Verify your visa eligibility, passport validity, and any travel restrictions before booking flights.
termsPage.bullets5Item3: Maintain appropriate medical insurance. Most plans don't cover elective international care.
termsPage.bullets5Item4: Pay hospitals directly. We never handle clinical payments ourselves.
termsPage.body6: Quotes are indicative until the destination hospital has reviewed your medical records in full. Final prices may adjust based on findings during pre-operative workup (imaging in-country, blood work, cardiac clearance, etc.). Any material change of ≥5% to the quote must be disclosed in writing before you commit.
termsPage.body7: We're a coordinator; we are not the operating entity. Your clinical contract is between you and the destination hospital. Their malpractice coverage, complication indemnity, and dispute-resolution processes apply. We disclose these terms on every hospital we match you to.
termsPage.body8: Second opinions are reviews of submitted records by senior specialists on our panel. They are for your consideration and do not constitute treatment or a substitute for an in-person consultation. Decisions to proceed, modify, or decline treatment remain yours in consultation with your treating doctor.
termsPage.body9: We don't charge you deposits. Any deposits paid to hospitals follow that hospital's refund policy, which we require in writing before you pay. Typical terms: full refund if cancelled >14 days before surgery (less processing fee), 50–70% refund 3–14 days before, case-by-case within 72 hours. Medical-reason cancellations (fever, abnormal labs) are typically handled without penalty — get this specific language in writing.
termsPage.body10: We provide coordination services on an "as is" basis. Our maximum aggregate liability to you is limited to the coordination fee we received from the hospital for your case, or US$1,000, whichever is greater. This does not limit our liability for gross negligence, wilful misconduct, or death and personal injury under applicable law.
termsPage.body11: You agree to indemnify us against third-party claims arising from inaccurate information you provided or activities clearly outside the scope of our coordination services.
termsPage.body12: These terms are governed by the laws of Delaware, USA, where MedCasts is incorporated. Disputes go first to good-faith negotiation, then mediation, then binding arbitration under AAA rules. You retain the right to bring claims before your local consumer-protection body where applicable law permits.
termsPage.body13: Content on this site (editorial articles, hospital descriptions, medical panel reviews, data compilations) is our intellectual property. You may share individual articles for non-commercial personal use. Republishing at scale, scraping, or retraining AI models on this content requires written permission.
termsPage.body14: Information here — hospital descriptions, treatment guides, cost ranges, blog posts — is educational, not medical advice. It doesn't establish a doctor-patient relationship. Before acting on anything: consult your doctor.

editorialPage.seoTitle: Editorial Policy — How We Source & Review
editorialPage.seoDescription: How MedCasts researches, reviews, cites, and updates the medical information on this site. Written for patients who need to know whether to trust what they read.
editorialPage.lede: Medical-tourism websites have a bad reputation, earned mostly. Lots of AI-generated content, stale prices, unnamed 'specialists', fake reviews. This page documents how we try not to be that — and where we still fall short so you know what to double-check.
editorialPage.h2Cadence: When we update, and how you'll know
editorialPage.listDirectoryPagesBody: (hospital profiles, doctor profiles, treatment summaries, cost pages) are generated from structured data — hospital websites, public registries (Wikipedia, Wikidata, OpenStreetMap, government portals), and hospital-supplied quote sheets. The copy is templated, not hand-written. We state this openly on each page by noting when prices were sampled and from how many hospitals.
editorialPage.listEditorialPagesBody: (blog posts, visa guides, destination overviews, condition and treatment explainers) are drafted by our in-house editorial team, then reviewed by a practising physician in the relevant specialty before publication. Reviewer name and specialty appear in the byline.
editorialPage.citationsIntro: For medical claims (procedure risks, success rates, recovery timelines), we cite at least one primary source. Acceptable primary sources are:
editorialPage.listCitPubMed: Peer-reviewed journals indexed on PubMed, published in the last 5 years where available
editorialPage.listCitGuidelines: National medical society guidelines (ACC, ESC, AUA, ACOG, equivalents)
editorialPage.listCitWHO: WHO, CDC, NICE, or equivalent public-health authority publications
editorialPage.listCitHospital: Hospital-supplied outcome data where the hospital publicly reports it (some partner hospitals publish annual outcome reports — we link to those)
editorialPage.citationsOutro: We don't cite other medical-tourism websites. Circular sourcing is how bad numbers spread.
editorialPage.pricingPara1: Prices on hospital and treatment pages reflect quote ranges sampled from partner-hospital quote sheets across a rolling six-month window. Individual quotes are case-specific and are not the published ranges — a patient with comorbidities or a complex anatomy will receive a different number. We flag the methodology on every cost page and request hospitals confirm published ranges before listing.
editorialPage.pricingPara2: We don't inflate prices to create a comparison arbitrage with our own service. Hospitals pay our coordination fee; patients see the same package price they'd see by contacting the hospital directly.
editorialPage.cadencePara1: Editorial pages carry a Last updated date and, separately, a Last reviewed date. "Updated" means a factual element changed (a visa rule, a regulation, a price band). "Reviewed" means a physician re-read the page and confirmed nothing is outdated, even if nothing was edited.
editorialPage.listCadenceVisa: Visa guides: re-reviewed quarterly, or whenever an embassy announces a rule change
editorialPage.listCadenceCost: Cost pages: re-priced every six months minimum
editorialPage.listCadenceHospital: Hospital profiles: re-checked annually against the accrediting body registry
editorialPage.listCadenceTreatment: Condition / treatment explainers: reviewed annually unless flagged by a physician reviewer
editorialPage.correctionsPara: If you find an error — a stale price, an out-of-date visa rule, a doctor profile that misrepresents credentials — email medcastsdigital@gmail.com. Corrections acknowledge within 2 working days, with a dated correction note at the bottom of the page if the change is material. We don't silently edit live pages to erase prior errors.
editorialPage.adsPara1: We don't run ads. We don't accept affiliate fees from hospitals for placement or sort order on listing pages. Listing sort order on /hospitals is by rating and review count, filterable by country and specialty — not by ad spend. Hospitals that pay our partnership fee are disclosed on hospital profile pages.
editorialPage.adsPara2: When a hospital is partnered with us, that does not elevate them on listing or comparison pages. It only means we can coordinate quotes, travel, and post-op support for them. Non-partner hospitals remain listed and visible.
editorialPage.aiPara1: We use automation. Directory pages — 9,000+ hospital profiles, 800+ doctor profiles, 80+ treatment pages — are generated by combining structured data with templated copy. This is how we cover the long tail. Editorial content is not AI-generated; it's drafted by humans and reviewed by physicians.
editorialPage.aiPara2: Where directory copy is automated, you'll notice: short, structural, factual. Where copy is written by our editorial team, it reads differently. We don't try to pass one off as the other.
editorialPage.listNever1: Publish outcome statistics without citing the source
editorialPage.listNever2: Write in the name of a physician who hasn't reviewed the content
editorialPage.listNever3: Manufacture patient testimonials (real testimonials cite the patient's country, treatment, and year)
editorialPage.listNever4: Recommend a specific surgeon outside of a written second-opinion or quote workflow with your records on file
editorialPage.leadershipPara: Medical review is led by rotating specialists from our partner hospitals. Each editorial piece carries a Reviewed by Dr. [Name], [Credential], [Hospital] byline. If you see one without a byline, that's a mistake — email us and we'll fix it.
editorialPage.foundErrorText: Email medcastsdigital@gmail.com — acknowledged in 2 working days, dated correction note if material.

insurancePage.faqQ1: Can I use my international insurance at MedCasts partner hospitals?
insurancePage.faqA1: Yes — we work with 20+ international insurers. Cashless settlement depends on the insurer and destination hospital; we handle pre-authorization paperwork on your behalf.
insurancePage.faqQ2: What if my policy requires reimbursement rather than cashless?
insurancePage.faqA2: We provide all itemised invoices, discharge summaries, diagnostic reports, and claim-ready documentation in English within 5 business days of discharge.
insurancePage.faqQ3: Does overseas medical tourism affect my premium?
insurancePage.faqA3: No. MedCasts pricing is typically 60-80% below US / UK standards, so insurers often encourage overseas treatment for planned procedures.
insurancePage.faqQ4: What isn't covered by standard international policies?
insurancePage.faqA4: Cosmetic procedures, fertility treatment, and experimental therapies are usually out-of-pocket. Dental is covered only with dental add-ons. We flag these upfront in your quote.
insurancePage.insuranceCtaText: Share your policy card. We confirm in 24 hours.
insurancePage.howHeading: How insurance for medical travel actually works
insurancePage.howStep1Desc: Most domestic insurance excludes elective international procedures. Some international policies (Cigna Global, Allianz Care, AXA, Bupa Global) reimburse at JCI hospitals. Confirm pre-authorization requirements.
insurancePage.howStep2Desc: If your insurer covers any portion, pre-auth is typically required. We handle the documentation: clinical justification, hospital quotes, expected outcome data.
insurancePage.howStep3Desc: Cashless direct-billing arrangements exist with select Gulf insurers. Most international cases are reimbursement: you pay, then submit for partial recovery.
insurancePage.howStep4Desc: Itemized invoices with diagnosis (ICD-10) and procedure (CPT) codes, discharge summary, operative note, pathology. Translation may be required.
insurancePage.howStep5Desc: Standard travel insurance covers emergency medical events during your trip — not the planned procedure. Worth carrying for unrelated emergencies (which can happen).
insurancePage.howOutroNote: Don't plan international travel based primarily on insurance reimbursement. The cost savings vs domestic care are usually large enough that the trip makes sense without insurance — any reimbursement is a bonus.
insurancePage.wteItem1Desc: Most insurance excludes elective international. Some self-funded employer plans have explicit international benefits (notably WalMart, Lowe's). HSA/FSA funds work for qualified expenses. Tax deduction available above 7.5% AGI threshold.
insurancePage.wteItem2Desc: NHS doesn't cover elective international. Private UK insurance typically excludes — some policies have global cover with strict pre-auth.
insurancePage.wteItem3Desc: Cross-Border Healthcare Directive provides reimbursement at home-country rates within EU. Outside-EU travel (Turkey, India) typically not covered.
insurancePage.wteItem4Desc: Strong direct-billing arrangements with select Gulf insurers (Daman, Oman Insurance, Bupa Arabia). Cashless service common at major hospitals.
insurancePage.wteItem5Desc: Cosmetic-only procedures, fertility (sometimes excluded), travel costs, accommodation. Verify exclusions before relying on coverage.

hospitalsPage.howHeading: How to use this hospital directory
hospitalsPage.howStep1Desc: 9 active destination countries. India for highest volume + value, Turkey for cosmetic/dental/bariatric, Thailand for service experience, Germany/Korea for complex cases, UAE for premium.
hospitalsPage.howStep2Desc: JCI is the strongest international signal. Combined with country-specific accreditations (NABH, HA, KOIHA) is stronger still. Don't filter purely on accreditation — combine with surgeon volume.
hospitalsPage.howStep3Desc: Use the compare tool to put 3 hospitals side-by-side. Look at: bed count, established year, accreditations, specialty count, sample pricing.
hospitalsPage.howStep4Desc: Click into the hospital's specific department for your case. Hospital-wide reputation matters less than department-specific volume on your procedure.

hospitalsPage.whatHeading: What separates a good hospital from a great one
hospitalsPage.whatItem1Desc: Institutional reputation can hide wide variation between surgeons. Ask for the specific surgeon's annual case volume on your exact procedure.
hospitalsPage.whatItem2Desc: JCI + country-specific (NABH/HA/KOIHA) + ISO 9001 is a triangulated quality signal. Single accreditation is a baseline.
hospitalsPage.whatItem3Desc: Programs that publish 30-day mortality, revision rates, and complication rates are typically the strongest.
hospitalsPage.whatItem4Desc: For complex procedures, ICU step-down with cardiac/neuro intensivist on call 24/7 makes the difference between safe and risky.
hospitalsPage.whatItem5Desc: Multilingual coordinators, dedicated international wings, post-discharge telemedicine — these aren't luxury; they're risk management.
hospitalsPage.whatItem6Desc: The best programs decline cases that don't fit them. A program willing to take any case is sometimes a program operating at the margin.

doctorsPage.seoDescription: Search board-certified specialists across 9 medical destinations. Filter by specialty, country, or city. Every profile includes verified credentials, patient volume, and consultation fees.

doctorsPage.howHeading: How to evaluate surgeons in this directory
doctorsPage.step1Desc: Don't search 'cardiac surgeon' — search 'mitral valve repair surgeon'. Sub-specialty experience matters more than general specialty designation.
doctorsPage.step2Desc: Look for surgeons doing 100+ of your specific procedure annually. Below 50/year, complications rates measurably increase across most procedures.
doctorsPage.step3Desc: Board certification, fellowship training, hospital privileges, peer-reviewed publications. Cross-check on PubMed, Google Scholar, ORCID.
doctorsPage.step4Desc: Look for specifics — procedure name, date, outcomes at 6/12 months. Generic 'great surgeon' testimonials are less informative than specific case stories.
doctorsPage.step5Desc: Before booking, talk to the surgeon directly (not just sales). 20-30 minutes is enough to assess communication quality and case-specific fit.
doctorsPage.howOutro: Programs vary in surgeon assignment. Confirm before any procedure that the specific surgeon you've consulted with is the one performing your case.
doctorsPage.wteHeading: What predicts a good surgical outcome
doctorsPage.wte1Desc: Surgeon volume on the specific procedure is the strongest single predictor of outcomes — across cardiac, orthopedic, urologic, and oncologic surgery.
doctorsPage.wte2Desc: A 'spine surgeon' doing 100 procedures a year — but spread across cervical, lumbar, deformity, oncologic — is different from a deformity-focused surgeon doing 100 scoliosis cases. Match precisely.
doctorsPage.wte3Desc: Best surgeons work in programs with strong tumor boards (oncology), heart teams (cardiac), or spine conferences. Solo cowboys often produce average outcomes.
doctorsPage.wte4Desc: Surgeons who explain trade-offs clearly, set realistic expectations, and respond to questions are typically the same ones who manage complications well.
doctorsPage.wte5Desc: The best surgeons know what they're not great at. Surgeons who claim equal expertise across many sub-specialties are sometimes the ones with shallow expertise everywhere.
doctorsPage.wte6Desc: Surgeons who personally follow up post-op are typically more invested in outcomes than those who hand off to junior staff or leave it entirely to coordinators.

treatmentsPage.howStep2Desc: Each treatment page has candidacy criteria, recovery timeline, surgeon questions, red flags. Read these before getting quotes.
treatmentsPage.howStep3Desc: Same procedure varies 2-5× across destinations. See the cost-by-country page for your treatment to understand the price-quality matrix.
treatmentsPage.howStep4Desc: For your procedure, the best destination depends on case complexity. Routine = India top-tier; complex = Germany or premium Asian.
treatmentsPage.howStep5Desc: Once you've narrowed to 1-2 destinations, request itemized quotes from 3-4 hospitals. Compare on equal scope.
treatmentsPage.wteHeading: The questions that matter most before any procedure
treatmentsPage.wte1Desc: Many procedures are over-recommended. Conservative management adequately tried? Second opinion confirming the recommendation? Both should be yes before committing.
treatmentsPage.wte2Label: What does the surgeon do specifically?
treatmentsPage.wte2Desc: Their personal annual case volume on this specific procedure. Below 50/year, complications run measurably higher.
treatmentsPage.wte3Desc: Best case, expected case, worst case. Programs that present only the best case are managing expectations poorly.
treatmentsPage.wte4Desc: Day-by-day timeline, return-to-activity windows. Programs that claim 'rapid recovery' without specifics are marketing.
treatmentsPage.wte5Desc: Revision policy, complications coverage, telemedicine follow-up duration. Get answers in writing before booking.
treatmentsPage.wte6Desc: Itemized quote with exclusions clearly listed. Total trip cost typically 1.5-2.5× the procedure quote.

medicalTourismCompaniesPage.seoTitle: Medical Tourism Companies — How to Choose a Facilitator
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.seoDescription: What medical tourism companies and facilitators actually do, the four types, how to vet one, the red flags to avoid, and how a transparent coordinator should work.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.heroLede: Before you hand a company your medical records, understand what a medical tourism company is, the four kinds you'll meet, and the five tests that separate a real coordinator from a lead broker.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.introParagraph: A medical tourism company sits between a patient in one country and a hospital in another. The good ones save you months of research and protect you from expensive mistakes. The bad ones quietly steer you to whoever pays them the most. The category word — "company", "facilitator", "agency", "coordinator" — tells you almost nothing. How they answer five questions tells you everything.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.type1Body: Run by the hospital itself. Fast and direct, but single-vendor by design — they will never tell you another hospital is a better fit, and they can't compare prices for you.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.type2Body: Independent of any one hospital. They shortlist hospitals and surgeons, handle quotes, visas and logistics, and stay with you end-to-end. Quality depends entirely on whether they disclose how they're paid.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.type3Body: Large directories where clinics buy listings or leads. Useful for breadth, but ranking often reflects ad spend, not outcomes — and there's usually no one accountable after you book.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.type4Body: Collect your enquiry and sell it to several clinics at once. You'll be called by sales teams, not clinicians. Cheap to start, but no continuity and no independent advocate.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.howHeading: Five tests for any medical tourism company
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.step1Desc: Ask which accreditations the hospitals hold — JCI, ISO 9001, and the national regulator. A company that can't name them, or sends you to unaccredited clinics, has failed the first test.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.step2Desc: Get it in writing: do you pay a coordination fee, or does the hospital pay them a commission? Either is fine. A refusal to say is not.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.step3Desc: A real coordinator gives you two or three hospitals with trade-offs. A company that only ever recommends one is selling that one, not advising you.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.step4Desc: Surgeon fee, hospital stay, implants, diagnostics, follow-up — line by line. Bundled 'all-inclusive' numbers hide where the markup lives.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.step5Desc: Confirm a named person owns your case post-procedure, and how to reach them if there's a complication once you're home. No after-care contact is a red flag.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.howOutroNote: A company that passes all five will rarely be the cheapest quote in your inbox. It will almost always be the cheapest outcome.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.expectHeading: Red flags worth walking away from
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.flag1Desc: "This price is only good today" is a sales tactic, not a medical one. Surgery decisions don't expire in 24 hours.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.flag2Desc: If every enquiry — whatever the condition — routes to the same hospital, you're being steered, not advised.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.flag3Desc: A single bundled figure with no breakdown means you can't see the markup, and can't compare like-for-like.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.flag4Desc: Being asked for full medical records before the company will disclose how it's paid or which hospitals it uses.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.flag5Desc: Success rates and outcome guarantees should come from a surgeon, in a consultation — never from a coordinator's call centre.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.flag6Desc: If you can't get a clear answer on who handles complications once you've flown home, assume the answer is no one.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.standsParagraph: MedCasts is a medical-travel coordinator, not a clinician and not a hospital. We match international patients to accredited hospitals and surgeons across nine destinations. We shortlist more than one hospital, we itemise quotes, and our directory and treatment content are reviewed by an independent medical panel. We're not a perfect category — no facilitator is — but the five tests above are the ones we hold ourselves to, and the ones we'd want you to hold us to.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.faq1Q: What does a medical tourism company actually do?
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.faq1A: A medical tourism company — also called a facilitator or coordinator — helps an international patient plan treatment abroad. That typically means shortlisting accredited hospitals and surgeons, collecting itemised quotes, arranging the medical visa, booking travel and accommodation, and acting as a single point of contact before, during and after the procedure. It does not replace your doctor: a good facilitator coordinates care, it does not deliver it.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.faq2Q: How are medical tourism companies paid?
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.faq2A: There are two honest models. Some charge the patient a flat coordination fee. Others are paid a referral commission by the hospital. The model itself is not the problem — hidden commission is. Ask any company to put its payment model in writing before you share medical records. If they will not, treat that as a decision.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.faq3Q: Are medical tourism facilitators safe to use?
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.faq3A: A facilitator is as safe as the hospitals it sends you to and the transparency it operates with. The risk is not the concept — it is single-vendor steering, undisclosed markup, and no accountability once you have paid. Choose a company that works with accredited hospitals, discloses how it earns, and stays reachable after discharge.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.faq4Q: How do I compare medical tourism companies?
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.faq4A: Judge them on five things: hospital accreditation (JCI, ISO and national bodies), whether they disclose how they are paid, whether they will give you more than one hospital option, whether quotes are itemised rather than bundled, and whether a named person owns your case after the procedure. A company that scores well on all five is rare — and worth far more than the cheapest quote.
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.faq5Q: Is MedCasts a medical tourism company?
medicalTourismCompaniesPage.faq5A: MedCasts is a medical-travel coordinator. We are not clinicians and we are not a hospital — we match international patients to accredited hospitals and surgeons across nine destinations, with transparent pricing and one point of contact end-to-end. Our directory, hospital data and treatment content are reviewed by an independent medical panel.

pricingIndexPage.seoDescription: Median package pricing for {treatmentsCovered} treatments across {countriesCovered} destination countries. Open data methodology, {pairsCount} country × treatment pairs. Free to cite.
pricingIndexPage.hereLede: Real package pricing for {treatmentsCovered} planned procedures across {countriesCovered} destination countries, aggregated from {hospitalOfferings} hospital offerings. Free to cite, CSV and JSON downloads below, methodology disclosed.
pricingIndexPage.emptyStateText: Price data is currently being aggregated. Check back soon, or download the
pricingIndexPage.methodologyP1: All figures are USD package prices — the all-inclusive quote a hospital provides for an international patient covering surgeon + OR + hospital stay + standard pre/post-op imaging and meds, before international travel and visa costs.
pricingIndexPage.methodologyP2: For each (country × treatment) pair we require at least three active hospital offerings. The median is computed as the 50th percentile of each hospital's midpoint (min + max / 2). This suppresses anecdotal outliers. Pairs with fewer than three offerings are excluded rather than shown with low confidence.
pricingIndexPage.methodologyP3: Excluded: robotic-assisted variants when standard surgery is the comparison baseline, re-do / revision cases (different clinical complexity), paediatric variants, research protocols with trial sponsorship. All currency conversions at the ECB daily reference rate captured on the first of each quarter.
pricingIndexPage.methodologyP4: What we don't claim: these are not personalised quotes. Real quotes depend on the individual case workup, travel dates, room class, and whether the hospital offers a fixed package or itemised billing. Use the index to size the ballpark; request a real quote through a coordinator before booking.
pricingIndexPage.methodologyP5: Raw data, including per-hospital rows, is available as CSV and JSON. We refresh this dataset quarterly; the download reflects the last refresh date stamped in the file.

securityPage.seoDescription: How to report a security issue to MedCasts. Scope, timeline, recognition, and what we won't accept.
securityPage.leadParagraph: MedCasts coordinates planned medical travel for international patients — the data we hold (case summaries, IDs, payment intent, treatment plans) is sensitive. If you find a vulnerability, we want to hear from you.
securityPage.reportItem1: A short summary of the issue + impact
securityPage.reportItem2: Steps to reproduce — minimal payload, no scraping
securityPage.reportItem3: Optional PGP key (we'll set up encrypted reply if requested)
securityPage.urgentNote: For urgent issues (active exploit), prefix the subject with [CRITICAL] — paged 24/7. Routine reports get a written acknowledgement within 2 business days and an initial assessment within 5.
securityPage.inScopeItem5: Stored data exposure (PHI, payment intent, contact details)
securityPage.inScopeItem7: Stored XSS / DOM XSS in admin or patient portal
securityPage.outOfScopeItem1: Self-XSS or social-engineering of MedCasts staff
securityPage.outOfScopeItem2: Vulnerabilities in third-party services we use (report to them)
securityPage.outOfScopeItem3: Best-practice findings without an exploit chain (missing security headers on a page that ships them everywhere else, etc.)
securityPage.outOfScopeItem4: Rate-limit bypasses on read-only public endpoints
securityPage.outOfScopeItem5: Outdated software disclosure with no exploit
securityPage.outOfScopeItem6: Spam / abuse via the inquiry form (CSRF + rate-limit already gate it)
securityPage.whatWeAskItem1Rest: If you find an exposure, stop, document, and report. We'll reproduce on our side.
securityPage.whatWeAskItem2: Don't run automated scanners against production. Test on a fork or against the local dev server (instructions in the project README).
securityPage.whatWeAskItem3: Don't disclose publicly until we've shipped a fix or we've agreed on a coordinated date (default 90 days).
securityPage.whatWeAskItem4: One report per issue. Bundling chains is fine.
securityPage.recognitionParagraph: We run a non-monetary acknowledgement program — every confirmed report gets a write-up on this page (with researcher name + report date, opt-in) and a reference letter for portfolio use. We're a small team and don't run a paid bounty program yet; we'll be transparent if that changes.

calculatorPage.howItWorksStep1Desc: Search 88 procedures across 15 specialties. We use the same procedure naming convention as the WHO ICD-11 catalog and major US billing codes — so 'CABG' and 'coronary artery bypass grafting' both find the same entry.
calculatorPage.howItWorksStep2Desc: 9 destination countries. Each has a baseline pricing structure reflecting local cost of care, surgeon compensation, and currency. We don't include US/UK/Australia in this calculator (cost of care is fundamentally different).
calculatorPage.howItWorksStep3Desc: We show low, mid, and high price ranges by hospital tier within the destination. Mid-range is what most patients actually pay; the low range is bottom-tier programs we'd usually steer away from.
calculatorPage.howItWorksStep4Desc: If you proceed, we show 3-5 specific hospital options with current pricing. These are itemized quotes — surgeon fee, implant, hospital stay, anesthesia broken out — not package marketing.
calculatorPage.howItWorksOutroNote: Calculator shows ranges based on hospital-reported pricing collected over the past 90 days. Final cost depends on your specific case complexity, implant choice, length of stay, and destination program. Get an itemized quote for binding pricing.
calculatorPage.whatToExpectItem1Desc: Bottom-tier programs in the destination. Often technically capable but lacking some quality infrastructure (limited ICU, less experienced surgeons on rare cases). For routine procedures, sometimes appropriate; for complex cases, we generally steer toward mid-tier.
calculatorPage.whatToExpectItem2Desc: Where most international patients land. Top-tier programs with substantial international-patient experience, full clinical infrastructure, and transparent pricing. The 'right answer' for most cases.
calculatorPage.whatToExpectItem3Desc: Premium programs (often featured Western-affiliate hospitals or new-wave premium destinations). Charge a premium for amenities and concierge experience; clinical outcomes typically not better than mid-range.
calculatorPage.whatToExpectItem4Desc: Travel costs, accommodation, meals, attendant logistics, complications, follow-up imaging, post-op medications. Real total trip cost typically 1.5-2.5× the procedure quote.

treatmentDetailPage.phase1Body: Surgical day plus monitored ward recovery. Pain managed by anesthesia team. First post-op imaging or labs typically same day or next morning.
treatmentDetailPage.phase2Title: Day {start}–{end}: out of hospital, in destination
treatmentDetailPage.phase2Body: Discharged to a serviced apartment or recovery hotel near the hospital. Two follow-up reviews; suture or staple removal where applicable. Most patients walk short distances and self-cater.
treatmentDetailPage.phase3Body: Surgeon signs off on a fitness-to-fly letter once vitals and wound healing are within range. Compression stockings and a flight-day medication plan provided. We coordinate handover with your home doctor.
treatmentDetailPage.phase4Body: Phased return to work, exercise and travel. Tele-follow-ups at 30, 60 and 90 days. Imaging review at 90 days where the protocol calls for it; most patients are signed off in person locally.
treatmentDetailPage.recoveryTimelineDesc: A typical timeline based on hospital-issued discharge protocols and the cases we coordinate. Your case manager will confirm exact dates against your surgeon's plan.

treatmentDetailPage.contraindicationsBody: We turn cases away when traveling for {name} doesn't make medical or logistical sense. The most common reasons are below — your case manager screens against these on the first review.
treatmentDetailPage.ci1A: Active heart failure, uncontrolled diabetes (HbA1c > 9), or recent stroke. We'll ask for stabilisation locally before clearing for travel.
treatmentDetailPage.ci2A: Conditions where every week of delay materially worsens outcome. Travel logistics — visa, flights, post-op stay — usually adds 2–4 weeks vs. local care.
treatmentDetailPage.ci3A: Anyone who can't tolerate a 4-hour flight at week 2 (e.g. severe COPD, recent DVT history, certain spine procedures) shouldn't be doing this trip.
treatmentDetailPage.ci4A: For most procedures here we require an adult attendant for the first 14 days. We'll help apply for an attendant visa where the destination requires it.
treatmentDetailPage.ci5A: If your insurer fully covers this procedure locally with no waiting list, traveling rarely beats the math. Ask us to compare; we'll say so.
treatmentDetailPage.ci6Q: Outcomes tracker says local volume is fine
treatmentDetailPage.ci6A: If you live near a high-volume centre that does this case 100+ times a year, the volume premium of traveling is small. We'd rather you stay home with that team.

treatmentRecoveryPage.ledePara: What to expect after {treatmentName}: hospital stay, the days near the hospital, when it's safe to fly home, and the return to normal life around day {R}. A timeline to plan around — your surgeon's clearance is always the final word.
treatmentRecoveryPage.phase1BodyDayCase: Day-case procedure — you go home the same day once observation clears. Expect monitored recovery from anaesthesia, pain control, and discharge instructions before you leave.
treatmentRecoveryPage.phase1BodyHospital: Monitored recovery: pain control, wound and vital-sign checks, and early mobilisation. The care team confirms you can eat, move and manage pain before discharge.
treatmentRecoveryPage.phase2Body: International patients stay near the hospital for the first post-discharge review. Wound checks, medication adjustment, and the green light before any longer travel happen in this window.
treatmentRecoveryPage.phase3Body: Gradual return of energy and mobility. Light daily activity resumes; strenuous activity, heavy lifting and driving are still restricted. Most discomfort settles across this phase.
treatmentRecoveryPage.phase4Body: By about day {R}, most patients are back to desk work and routine daily life. Your surgeon's specific clearance — not the calendar — is what matters; follow their sign-off.
treatmentRecoveryPage.phase5Body: Full strength, final result and complete tissue healing continue past the return-to-normal point — often several more weeks. Keep follow-up appointments and report anything unexpected.
treatmentRecoveryPage.fitToFlyH3: Plan your flight home for day {from}–{to}, not earlier
treatmentRecoveryPage.fitToFlyBody: Long-haul flights raise clot risk during recovery, and cabin pressure can affect healing tissue and air-containing spaces. Book a flexible return ticket, keep accommodation near the hospital until the first review, and get written fit-to-fly clearance from your treating surgeon before you travel.
treatmentRecoveryPage.redFlagsDisclaimer: This is general guidance, not medical advice — your discharge instructions and surgeon override anything here. When in doubt, contact your care team or local emergency services.
treatmentRecoveryPage.faqA1DayCase: Most patients are back to routine daily activity around day {R}. It is a day-case procedure, followed by a staged return over the following weeks. Full strength and the final result continue beyond day {R}. Your surgeon's clearance — not the calendar — is the real signal.
treatmentRecoveryPage.faqA1Hospital: Most patients are back to routine daily activity around day {R}. The hospital stay is about {H} {nights}, followed by a staged return over the following weeks. Full strength and the final result continue beyond day {R}. Your surgeon's clearance — not the calendar — is the real signal.
treatmentRecoveryPage.faqQ2: When can I fly home after {treatmentName}?
treatmentRecoveryPage.faqA2: Most international patients are cleared to fly roughly {from}–{to} days after the procedure, once the first post-discharge review is done. Long-haul flights carry a clot risk during recovery — get explicit fit-to-fly sign-off from your treating surgeon before booking, and plan accommodation near the hospital until then.
treatmentRecoveryPage.faqQ3: When can I return to work?
treatmentRecoveryPage.faqA3: Desk or light work is usually possible around day {R}; physically demanding work takes longer and depends on your surgeon's clearance. Build a buffer into your plans rather than booking to the minimum.
treatmentRecoveryPage.faqA4: Some discomfort is normal and is managed with prescribed medication that is stepped down as you heal. Pain that worsens, or isn't controlled by your medication, is not normal — contact your care team.
treatmentRecoveryPage.faqQ5: What follow-up will I need back home?
treatmentRecoveryPage.faqA5WithSpecialty: Before you leave, get a full discharge summary, imaging, and a medication list to hand to your local doctor. Arrange {specialtyName} follow-up locally for ongoing checks. We help coordinate this handover.
treatmentRecoveryPage.faqA5NoSpecialty: Before you leave, get a full discharge summary, imaging, and a medication list to hand to your local doctor. Arrange specialist follow-up locally for ongoing checks. We help coordinate this handover.

costDetailPage.factorsHeading: Six levers that shift the quote
costDetailPage.factorsLede: Two quotes from the same hospital can differ by 40% once you drill into the details below. Ask your case manager to break out each line.
costDetailPage.factorSurgeonSeniorityBody: Senior consultants with 20+ years and high procedure counts command 20-40% above junior attendings for the same operation.
costDetailPage.factorHospitalTierBody: Flagship JCI-accredited facilities cost more than local tier-2 hospitals, even for identical procedures. The gap is usually 30-60%.
costDetailPage.factorRoomCategoryBody: Private-room vs twin-share vs deluxe suite can shift total package cost by 10-25% on longer admissions.
costDetailPage.factorImplantBrandBody: For joint replacement, cardiac valves, or dental implants, the device brand alone can change the bill by $1,500-$4,000.
costDetailPage.factorLengthOfStayBody: Complications or unplanned ICU days are the biggest variance driver. Ask for the per-diem overage rate upfront.
costDetailPage.factorPreOpWorkupBody: Imaging and labs done overseas aren't always re-done locally. If they are, budget 8-15% extra.
costDetailPage.includedDischargeMeds: Discharge medications for the admission period
costDetailPage.extraFollowUpTeleconsults: Follow-up teleconsults after the first 30 days
costDetailPage.faqHeading: Questions that come up a lot
costDetailPage.faq1Answer: Yes — at JCI-accredited facilities. The variable isn't country; it's surgeon and hospital. Ask for surgeon-specific procedure volume (aim for 100+ per year for elective work) before booking.
costDetailPage.faq2Question: How long do I need to stay?
costDetailPage.faq2AnswerWithDays: {inpatientDays} inpatient days is typical{recoveryDays} Build in a few buffer days in case labs or imaging flag something.
costDetailPage.faq2RecoveryClause: , plus ~{recoveryDays} days local recovery before you're cleared to fly.
costDetailPage.faq2AnswerNoDays: Stay length varies by case. Plan around the typical inpatient window plus 3-7 recovery days before your flight home.
costDetailPage.faq3Question: Does my insurance cover treatment abroad?
costDetailPage.faq3Answer: Some international policies (Cigna, Bupa, Allianz, AXA) reimburse at overseas JCI hospitals. Most domestic insurance doesn't. We confirm cashless vs reimbursement before admission — share your policy and we'll verify.
costDetailPage.faq4Question: What's included in the package price?
costDetailPage.faq4Answer: Typically: surgery fee, anaesthesia, standard room, standard implants, routine post-op imaging. Not typically included: airport transfer, hotel, complications, premium implants, extended ICU days. Quotes always show the split.
costDetailPage.faq5Question: How do I choose between countries?
costDetailPage.faq5Answer: For routine procedures, go on price + your visa ease. For complex cases, go on surgeon-specific volume and outcome data — which we request from each hospital before presenting quotes.
costDetailPage.faq6Question: Can I travel home right after?
costDetailPage.faq6Answer: Commercial air travel post-surgery depends on the procedure and the airline's medical-clearance policy. Most cardiac patients fly 10-14 days post-op; orthopedic patients 7-10 days; cosmetic 5-7 days. Your case manager will flag the specifics.

visaDetailPage.faq1ANo: Most nationalities can enter {countryName} visa-free or with visa-on-arrival for short elective procedures. For stays beyond 30 days or surgical cases requiring extension, a medical visa is recommended.
visaDetailPage.faq2Q: How long does the visa last?
visaDetailPage.faq2AAttendants: Family attendants can be included on related visa categories.
visaDetailPage.faq2AFallback: Typical medical visas for {countryName} last 60-90 days, often extendable. Confirm the latest rules with the embassy or your case manager.
visaDetailPage.faq3Q: Can family members travel with me?
visaDetailPage.faq3AYes: Yes — most destinations including {countryName} issue attendant visas for immediate family travelling with the patient. Relationship documentation is typically required.
visaDetailPage.faq3ANo: {countryName} does not have a dedicated attendant visa category — family members apply via standard tourist or visit visa.
visaDetailPage.faq4Q: What should I prepare before applying?
visaDetailPage.faq4A: Get your hospital's invitation letter in writing (not just email), translate civil documents if required, photograph your passport + photos in advance, and have 3-6 months of bank statements ready. Your case manager prepares most of this bundle for you.
visaDetailPage.faq5Q: Is MedCasts help with the visa included?
visaDetailPage.faq5A: Yes — visa invitation letter, documentation checklist, and embassy-appointment coordination are all part of the standard case-manager service. You handle the in-person appointment if one is required; we handle the paperwork bundle.
visaDetailPage.ctaBottomBody: We prepare the full bundle: hospital invitation, document checklist, embassy-appointment guidance, and itemized quotes from 3 accredited hospitals.
visaDetailPage.howItWorksHeading: How to apply for a medical visa to {countryName}
visaDetailPage.howStep1Desc: First step. The destination hospital issues a formal invitation letter on its letterhead, addressed to the embassy or consulate. We coordinate this through the partner hospital — typical turnaround 3-5 days.
visaDetailPage.howStep2Desc: Book an appointment at the {countryName} embassy or consulate in your country. Some destinations offer eVisa for medical purposes; verify eligibility for your nationality.
visaDetailPage.howStep3Desc: Standard package: passport (≥6 months validity), photos, hospital invitation, treatment cost estimate, accommodation proof, return flight tickets. Some destinations also require: medical history summary, prior treatment records, financial statements.
visaDetailPage.howStep4Desc: Submit at the appointment. Visa fees vary by country and processing time. Standard processing typically 5-15 business days; expedited where available 2-5 days.
visaDetailPage.howStep5Desc: Visa is typically issued for the duration of treatment + buffer (commonly 30-90 days). Attendant visas (1-2 family members) can be applied for in parallel.
visaDetailPage.howOutroNote: We handle the visa coordination as part of our standard service. Documents reviewed for completeness before submission. {countryName} embassy appointment booking guidance provided.
visaDetailPage.whatItem1Desc: Some embassies reject invitations that don't specify exact procedure, dates, and cost. Get specific letters, not generic ones.
visaDetailPage.whatItem2Desc: Embassies often require evidence of ability to pay (bank statements, treatment payment confirmation). Submit clear documentation up front.
visaDetailPage.whatItem3Desc: Tourist visa for treatment is technically improper at most destinations. Use medical visa specifically — even if processing takes longer.
visaDetailPage.whatItem4Desc: Don't apply for attendants as separate tourist visas; coordinate with the medical visa application. Both should reference the patient's invitation letter.
visaDetailPage.whatItem5Desc: Plan visa application 6-8 weeks before treatment date. Embassy holiday windows, document re-submission, or interview requests can extend timelines.
